site.title: bench
site.description: Run a team of coding agents without losing track of what they are doing.

pages.title: bench — run a team of coding agents, stay in control
pages.description: Your agents ship faster than you can keep track. Every task is a card, every agent gets its own worktree, every change waits as a PR. Nothing merges without you.

pages.title: Install and first run
pages.description: Untar bench into .task-manager/, run start.sh, and answer the three questions the first run asks.

pages.title: The five stages
pages.description: backlog, to-do, in-progress, review, done — the directory a task file sits in is its status, and there is no other source of truth.

pages.title: Task files
pages.description: A task is a markdown file with a numbered name and a short header. Status is the only field the board enforces.

pages.title: Claiming a card
pages.description: Claiming is moving: taking a card towards work is the commitment, and that is where ownership is recorded.

pages.title: Agents on the board
pages.description: Start work makes a worktree and a branch, runs the agent headless, and moves the card on the way it exits.

pages.title: PRs and review
pages.description: A card entering review gets a PR opened for it by the board; then review PR, copilot and act on PR, until it settles.

pages.title: Phases
pages.description: A phase is a card that lists its cards: Type: Phase, a ## Cards section in run order, and membership that runs one direction only.
pages.lede: The model, before anything runs: what a phase card is made of, how membership is written down, why it runs one direction only, and what the board flags when the list does not resolve.
pages.to: ### A phase runs itself, on a branch of its own

pages.title: Running a phase
pages.description: Each member branches from the phase's tip, runs headless, and merges back on green. Halt, never skip — and one PR into main at the end.
pages.lede: Everything between starting a phase and the one PR it ends with: where each member's branch is cut, what advances the run and what stops it, how a restarted board picks the phase back up, and what merging it does to the cards it carried.
pages.from: ### A phase runs itself, on a branch of its own
pages.to: ### A phase's members leave the Board view

pages.title: Where a phase is drawn
pages.description: The Board stops listing a phase's members and the phase card stands for them; the Phases view gives every phase a swimlane of its own.
pages.lede: A phase card stands for cards the kanban no longer lists. What the columns say instead, what the phase card owes in return, and the view that gives every phase a lane of its own.
pages.from: ### A phase's members leave the Board view

pages.title: Team mode
pages.description: BOARD_SYNC makes origin/main the truth and every board a converging replica: moves commit and push themselves, and a beat pulls what the other boards published.

pages.title: The three-layer law
pages.description: Core knows tasks, worktrees, PRs and events. Drivers know apps, adapters know agent vendors, local/ knows your project.

pages.title: Agent adapters
pages.description: Headless jobs run through an adapter, so the board works with coding agents other than Claude Code — and never sees a vendor's payloads.
pages.lede: The adapter is the layer that knows a coding agent. It launches one headless job, and translates that vendor's events into the board's own schema — which is what keeps every other line of core free of any particular agent.

pages.title: Settings
pages.description: Every BOARD_* setting with its default and what changing it does — generated from manager/core/.env.example, which is where the defaults live.
pages.lede: The whole of manager/core/.env.example, read out of the file itself on every build. Precedence runs process environment, then your manager/local/.env, then the defaults below — so a key you never copied is a key at the value shown here.

pages.title: The adapter contract
pages.description: The two executables an adapter is — run and wire — the three launch intents, the model passthrough, and the normalized event schema.
pages.lede: What you implement to put a different coding agent behind the board. Two executables, three launch intents, and one event schema; the shipped claude/ and opencode/ adapters are both of these read side by side.

pages.title: The driver contract
pages.description: manager/local/driver/start: the executable that launches your app from a task's worktree, and the four things the board asks of it.
pages.lede: How an app starts is project knowledge, so the board does not hold any of it: it runs one executable you write and owns it as a process group. Four env vars in, one line out when the app is up, and SIGTERM to park it.
pages.to: ## The activity bar and the archive

pages.title: The local-command contract
pages.description: manager/local/commands/: project chores run against a task's worktree, surfaced as chips on the cards that have a branch.
pages.lede: The driver's contract again, for the chores that belong to one checkout rather than to the app: migrations, reseeds, asset rebuilds. An executable in manager/local/commands/ becomes a chip on every card with a branch.
